Bun Official Bench Peer Test (buffer-read-write)

Peer method: the original bun problem bench/snippets/buffer-read-write.mjs is run with zero changes (the mitata numbers are an external reference); the SA peer program is written in SA only (FILL a 4096-byte pattern (i*37+11)&0xff plus 5000 full-scan sum verifications, check value 522240), compiled with sa build-js and run on both node / bun. All JS artifacts under test are SA-generated, with no hand-written mjs.

CombinationTime (before literal fix)Time (after fix)Result

3. Core finding: untyped integer literal domain pollution (proven)

  • The u32 slot version is actually slower than the u64 version on node (3108ms vs 2590ms). The profiler shows the u32 version spending 18.8% in __sa_BU and 17.8% in __sa_add (all BigInt paths).
  • Inspecting the generated code: r3 = __sa_ult(r2, 4096n) — untyped literals 4096/1/37/522240 in SA are all emitted as u64 (BigInt), so u32 register × BigInt literal = every iteration takes the mixed slow path plus conversion (megamorphic, not inlinable). The u64 version is faster precisely because it is uniformly BigInt-monomorphic.
  • Fixed (src/emit_js.zig resolveValueToJs): imm_i64/imm_u64 values whose magnitude fits in 32 bits are now emitted as Number, and only out-of-range values are emitted as BigInt. The runtime helpers dispatch on typeof; if either operand is BigInt the 64-bit path is taken, so semantics are unchanged; fully 32-bit expressions stay Number-monomorphic and inlinable. The u32 loop improves 3.1x on node / 9.7x on bun, with no regression in u64 summation. The slight rise of the u64-accumulation peer on node (2590→3091ms) is the literal Number→BigInt conversion tax, a small expected cost.
  • The domain cost on the SA basis (same SA workload, only the accumulation domain changed): on bun, u64 accumulation 11303ms vs u32 accumulation 589ms (19.2x); at roughly 8 helper calls per touch point, a single call in the Number domain on bun costs about 3~4ns. The main entry point of the 2x route is to keep reducing the per-element call count.
  • That bun's BigInt is slow is an SA-measured conclusion (not a hand-written micro-test): i64 summation bun 5274ms vs node 505ms (10.4x); the emitter accordingly added a __sa_use_dv64 switch (bun takes DataView, node keeps typed arrays), bringing SA's i64 loop on bun from 5274→4088ms.

4. buffer-fill peer (256KB fill + verification)

CombinationTime (single fill+verify pass, including cold start)Result
sa2js+node108msFILL OK
sa2js+bun96msFILL OK

Original bun problem reference: fill 16KB ≈ 335ns (0.02ns/B), fill 2MB ≈ 93µs (0.044ns/B, a single memset). The SA version makes about 7 helper calls per byte (ptr_add + store + slot access + comparison), a gap of about 3 orders of magnitude — the next optimization point for bulk memory operations is slot-to-local-variable promotion (loop counters bypass memory slots), which is orthogonal to the literal fix.

5. buffer-slice peer (64KB real copy + verification) + DCE confirmed

CombinationTime (single fill+copy+verify pass)Result
sa2js+node112msSLICE OK
sa2js+bun65msSLICE OK

The original bun slice(1M) shows 61ns — a 1MB copy cannot complete in 61ns, confirming dead-code elimination (the result is discarded and the copy is optimized away entirely; 64B/1KB/1M all show the same 55~75ns call overhead). So the bun slice numbers can serve only as a call-overhead reference, not as a copy-bandwidth reference. The SA version performs a real copy with verification (65~112ms/64KB). Estimated by memory bandwidth, an engine's real copy of 64KB takes about 3~10µs, so the SA gap is about 4 orders of magnitude, the same optimization direction as §4 (per-element helper calls → bulk memory semantics).

6. array-indexOf peer (1024 u32 linear search ×10000 + verification)

CombinationTime (2500 rounds × 4 needles × 1024 full scan)Result
sa2js+node466ms (45ns/element)FIND OK
sa2js+bun439ms (43ns/element)FIND OK

Original bun problem reference: includes (1024 ints) 245ns per call (needles rotate to prevent hoisting, average depth about 890, equivalent to about 0.3ns/element); indexOf (1024 ints) shows 3.31ns — a single 1024-element search cannot take 3ns, so it is DCE and cannot serve as a reference (the same class of problem as slice recurs). The SA version is a full scan plus branch recording (slightly different from indexOf's early exit, as noted); on branch-dense integer code node/bun are tied. The gap is about 150x, still a per-element helper call count problem (this loop has about 10 per element).

7. buffer-base64-decode peer (table-lookup decoding of 1.5MB + verification)

CombinationTime (500 rounds × 1024 groups × 4 characters)Result
sa2js+node269ms (179ns/decoded byte)B64 OK
sa2js+bun213ms (142ns/decoded byte)B64 OK

Original bun problem reference: decoding 1MiB of base64 takes about 250µs (0.24ns/B, a SIMD-class native codec, credibly real work); 64KiB containing 1% garbage about 25µs; a 512B small input 734ns (call overhead dominates). The SA version is pure-SA table-lookup decoding (a 256B decoding table built at runtime + per-group shl/or/lshr/and + 3-byte store-back + checksum), with about 35 helper calls per group. The gap is about 750x, still a call-density problem; the decoding table compresses 6 branches per character into 1 table lookup, proving that “data structures instead of branches” works in SA.

Incidental SA programming findings (proven): the bitwise-OR mnemonic is or, not bor (the latter pollutes the flattener and the error line misleads); the shift amount of shl/lshr must be a register (an immediate is illegal); the (register, register) form of and/or is legal; a const address cannot be taken directly (ptr_add &B64 is illegal), so input vectors should be constructed at runtime.

8. string-includes peer (4096B naive substring search for “jumps” ×500 + verification)

CombinationTime (early-exit hit @2000)Result
sa2js+node124ms (124ns/start position)STR OK
sa2js+bun110ms (110ns/start position)STR OK

Original bun problem reference: the short series are all 0.11ns — haystack and needle are both compile-time constants, so this is constant folding and none of them can serve as a reference; only long, miss at 9.45ns (4300B) is plausibly real (about 0.002ns/B, SIMD memchr class). The SA version compares 5 bytes per start position + a first-byte-mismatch fast path + early exit on hit (three levels of nesting + diamond merges; merge-point rule: a condition consumed by br must be Untracked on every path and cannot be !-ed again). The gap is about 3 orders of magnitude; the call-density problem remains.

10. escapeHTML peer (4KB×200 variable-length escaping + full-byte verification)

CombinationTime (input 819KB → output about 1.1MB)Result
sa2js+node1431ms (1.75µs/input byte)ESC OK

Original bun problem reference (Bun.escapeHTML, a bun-private API that node does not have): 57KB containing escapes about 69µs (1.2ns/B, SIMD); 56KB of pure pass-through about 3.3µs (0.06ns/B, zero-copy fast path); short inputs at 25~150ns are all call overhead. The SA version implements 5-character escaping itself (</>/&/"/&#39;, 6-way branching + variable-length output + a checksum over all output bytes); on branch-dense code bun overtakes node by nearly 5x (294 vs 1431ms, JSC's branch optimization wins). The gap is about 300x, likewise a call-density problem.

Peer list status (8/8 in the first class): read-write, fill, slice, indexOf, base64-decode, string-includes, from-hex, escapeHTML. The sorting class (array-sort/typed-array-sort) is missing for now: SA has no O(n log n) primitive, and an O(n²) loop cannot peer at bun's N; to be decided.

12. Hotspot distribution (after the literal fix, peer_rw32 node profiler)

Before the fix, the same positions were __sa_BU 18.8% + __sa_add 17.8% (the BigInt slow path); after the fix the ALU is inlined into main, and the remaining 4 calls are all semantically necessary (load / compare / addressing / slot reload). Slot promotion (moving acc/counters into local variables) would save only about 12%, so it is left alone; 2x still requires bulk memory semantics or proof-style full inlining.

13. Fused bulk primitives overtake (slope basis, after startup/warmup cancellation)

Per-element helpers can never catch up with a native codec on bulk operations, so the emitter added 9 fused primitives (sa_mfill/sa_mcopy/sa_msum_u8/sa_msum_u32/sa_mwrite_u8/sa_mfind_u32/sa_b64dec/sa_hexdec/sa_esc_html: one host call executes a tight loop or an engine intrinsic, at the same level as bun's Buffer underpinnings; all callable from SA, zero hand-written mjs). Methodology: a single wall time includes 30~90ms of startup + JIT warmup (the fill0 artifact, find single-run/slope differing 7x), so steady state is always reported with a two-point slope (the difference between REPS and 2×REPS).

Side note: 64-bit correctness. During the fusion work, rw3-batch (u64 accumulation 8.8e12) once went red, traced to the interaction between the emitter's literal Number-ization and the runtime |0 truncation — the interpreter has 64-bit semantics while the Number path is 32-bit. Fixed: add/sub drop the truncation (double is exact up to 2^53), mul/div/shift/bitwise ops/comparisons promote dynamically (small-value fast path, BigInt for large values), BigInt paths such as slt/sdiv get sign extension per the interpreter, and large extern returns are BigInt. All 20 peers + probes report green. Residual known boundary: the double exactness ceiling is 2^53 (actual sums within 16MB of memory are far below this). The cost of the win is about 130 extra lines in the emitter, all additive (new shims + helper branches), with no change to existing behavior.

Note: wasm once overtook native on read-write/indexOf, but measurement showed this was because the default sa build optimization level is conservative (not because wasmtime is stronger) — after rebuilding with --release-fast, native strikes back directly by 20~50x: read-write 20.5M scan 3.3ms (0.16ns/B, about 5x faster than the original bun problem's 0.77ns/B), find 10.2M searches 5.6ms (0.55ns/element) (LLVM vectorization fully on; all checksums pass, not DCE). Conclusion: the conservative default build is the main cause; for peak performance add --release-fast; native still has distance to a SIMD codec (for bulk codecs see the fusion section), but on loop-intensive workloads native already leads across the board.

15. Basis and next steps

  • All SA-side numbers on this page come from artifacts compiled from SA source; DCE statement: mitata single-expression benches are suspected of dead-code elimination, so absolute values follow the with-sink scale, while the relative ordering is consistent.
  • The remaining path to 2x is typing frontend literals by context (literals in a u32 context are emitted as Number); it involves all backends, requires joint native/wasm matrix testing, and is a separate project.
  • Next peer list (first-class peerable): buffer-fill, buffer-slice, buffer-compare, array-map, array-sort, string-includes, typed-array-sort, base64-decode, escapeHTML; on the memory side, a bun --heapStats streaming RSS comparison will be added afterwards.

16. Host codec in two in-place passes (measured 2026-10-12)

The old chain TextDecoder().decode(subarray) + Buffer.from + set took three passes plus two allocations; the new chain __sa_buf.toString('latin1') + __sa_buf.write(in-place) takes two passes with zero temporary allocations (emit_js.zig sa_b64dec/sa_hexdec). Fully equivalent on clean ASCII; short output (garbage input / out of bounds) now traps instead, eliminating silent truncation. Evidence peers: sci/demos/compare/peer_hex.sa(+5000)/peer_b64.sa(+5000), two-point slope (500→5000 runs × 64KB), all checksums pass (HEX 480000/4800000, B64 85000/850000).

peer (slope ns/B)bun original (same machine)Old chain nodeNew chain nodeOld chain bunNew chain bun

base64 64KB0.1490.510.21 (2.4x↑)0.360.25 (1.4x↑, 1.7x remaining)

The remainder = one latin1 snapshot pass + single-call overhead; a single bun intrinsic call is already the final form, and further reduction needs a batched call shape (decoding a larger block at once) or SIMD. The hex fusion item is unfrozen from here on (the pure-scalar route stays frozen).

17. Table-driven escape (measured 2026-10-12)

The old chain branched 6 times per byte; the new chain uses a 256B length-table fast path (a single branch for ordinary bytes) + a 1536B sequence rare path (emit_js.zig sa_esc_html). The per-byte output is isomorphic to the old chain, with the peer length + first/last bytes locked. Evidence peer: sci/demos/compare/peer_esc.sa(+500), 64KB / 8% escape density, two-point slope:

escape 64KB slopeOld chain nodeNew chain nodeOld chain bunNew chain bun

V8 branch prediction has already leveled the old chain (94% straight-through), so table loading gains nothing; JSC gets 1.4x. To squeeze a branching codec further still requires SIMD (see §13/§16).

18. Native explicit SIMD dual cores (measured 2026-10-12)

sa_std.zig sa_hexdec_simd (32 characters → a 16-byte vector + scalar tail, 3 unit tests in the same body) and sa_b64dec_simd (32→24 Mula interleave, 2 unit tests in the same body); the ABI goes through a sa_std.h declaration + a windows_unsupported annotation, with runtime_abi_check --platform both fully green (594 symbols). Evidence peers (native default tier, two-point slope, all checksums pass): sci/demos/compare/peer_hexn.sa(+5000) HEXN OK， peer_b64n.sa(+5000) B64N OK。

native slope ns/Bbun original (same machine)SIMD core
hex 64KB0.11~0.150.085 (overtakes by about 1.3~1.8x)
base64 64KB0.1490.068 (WIN 2.2x, §30 swizzle landed)

Toolchain pitfall: this toolchain's -OReleaseFast miscompiles negative-mask @shuffle (with a location-less error Assigned value does not match type of forward declaration); this was worked around with a concat relay + single-source positive masks, annotated in the code; probe reproduction + fix verification done.

Verdict (2026-10-13: the native b64 remainder of 1.5x is the end of the scalar horizon): a pure-core probe in /tmp (with no SA call overhead) confirms unroll×2 gains zero (0.236→0.236ns/B, backend-bound); the disassembly already shows 128 dense SIMD instructions (pshufb/paddb/movups class), with 9 shuffles/port5 as the structural floor; the u32-word trick still needs interleaving and cannot save the remaining ~35%. Reaching 2x requires the swizzle lookup route (an SSSE3-gated C kernel + exhaustive differencing; std.x86 does not exist in this toolchain), already made a separate project, with the acceptance line at bun's same-day 0.14ns/B. No further investment on the scalar side.

Follow-up verdict (2026-10-12: the swizzle project is closed, lookup-ceiling): three feasibility-probe results are conclusive — (1) all three LUT classification forms (direct add / sign flip / XOR) are proven unsolvable by program verification; the deadlock is the constraint-cycle conflict caused by '+'/'/' sharing a high nibble; (2) the disassembled hot loop has 15 pshufb + 5 pcmpeqb, port5 is already saturated, and an LUT would need 2 more shuffles, which would only add pressure or even regress; (3) the core slope is 0.203 vs bun's same-day 0.149, a 33% gap, while classification is only about 25% of the loop — free classification gives at most 1.33x, and a realistic LUT saves at most ~12% down to 0.19, mathematically short of the acceptance line. Conclusion: native b64's 1.5x is a double floor (scalar + lookup), permanently locked unless the whole core is rewritten at assembly level (outside the current basis); all probes are in /tmp, with zero code changes.

19. wasm SIMD128 inline core (measured 2026-10-13)

The wasm chain only recognizes in-module bitcode (a dangling extern gives wasm-ld: undefined symbol), so emit_llvm_llvmc_shim.c emits the v128 core inline (hex 16→8, b64 32→24 + scalar tail), defined only when the module references it (inside wasm_compat). +simd128 proved itself ineffective on scalar loops (247 vs 266ms), so the driver default became -mcpu=generic+simd128 (without this flag the vector core degenerates to scalar and is slower instead: 2.4ns/B). 21. Native substring-search bridge (measured 2026-10-13)

The pure-SA scalar loop in miss shape (4KB haystack + 64B needle, first-byte filter + per-position comparison) takes 28µs per call at the native default tier (6.8ns/B); the new extern sa_mfind_u8 (a direct call to Zig's std.mem.indexOf, returning the hay_len sentinel on miss to avoid the u64max literal overflow) takes 0.35µs per call in the same shape (0.085ns/B), 85x↑. 22. wasm hex overtake (measured 2026-10-13)

Case-fold classification (a single digit + single alpha test after c|0x20) replaces the three-interval diamond, isomorphic between vector and scalar; peer_hexn20000.sa (20000 points, stable within ±1%) + peer_hext.sa (tail transition) / peer_hexbad.sa (illegal input stops) lock correctness. Same-day back-to-back: our slope 10.03µs/64KB (0.153ns/B) against bun mitata 10.73µs (0.164ns/B), a 0.93x overtake. A methodology lesson noted separately: a naive hand-written timing loop (no warmup) once measured bun at 39µs (4x inflated); the basis must be mitata, compared on the same day.

23. find dual bridge + escape bridge rejected (measured 2026-10-13)

The sa_mfind_u8 scalar first-byte loop was changed to a single __sa_buf.indexOf(subarray) call (with an out-of-bounds hit guard and no Buffer fallback scalar loop): node 8.5µs→1.5µs (5.6x↑, tied-to-slightly-better than the node original's 2.9µs), bun 4µs→1.5µs (2.6x↑); a version of sa_mfind_u32 without the subarray allocation once measurably exploded — on miss, indexOf scans to the end of the window (the whole 16MB linear memory, 425µs per call); it was reverted to the bounded version (8.5s→73ms, about 100x recovered): subarray is load semantics (delimiting), not a removable allocation. Lesson: the mfind_u8 bridge is fast only because SA bump allocation keeps the needle near the haystack so it self-terminates (the 16MB full-scan behavior was also verified directly under node), while correctness rests entirely on the out-of-bounds guard, unrelated to speed. Evidence: peer_findj.sa(+5000)/peer_findjh.sa (the hit path), peer_findu32.sa(+5000)、peer_findr.sa（rotating needles 1000/512/1023/2048, three hits and one miss, guarding against engine hoisting); the guard logic was also verified directly under node.

Rejected item: the Bun.escapeHTML bridge, after a complete audit (the only difference over 0~255 is the single-quote style, for which a normalization plan exists), was measured and rejected — its string-in/string-out shape allocates 3 large strings per call, and the GC tax exceeds the SIMD gain (bridge 342µs vs table loop 155µs slope). The zero-allocation in-place table loop wins; a mis-measurement is also corrected: a latin1 snapshot on representative input averages only 18~22µs/64KB after warmup, actually an order of magnitude faster than utf8 (validation hell, 420µs+) — the reverse 10x conclusion from an early single cold measurement is void; on the codec side latin1 is both correct (garbage bytes visible 1:1, trappable) and fast, so nothing needs to change. Two lessons: at small granularity the allocation tax overwhelms everything (isomorphic to why Buffer.write wins); single cold-measurement numbers are always void — only the warmed-up average + two-point slope counts.

24. wasm substring-search memmem bridge (measured 2026-10-13)

The wasm chain does not recognize libsa (dangling symbols), so emit_sa_mfind_u8_wasm emits inline a thin memmem wrapper (empty needle → 0, over-long → miss, defined only when the forward declaration is missing; a dominance bug was also fixed: zext must land in diffblk rather than ret, which the LLVM verifier caught on the spot). Evidence: peer_findm100k.sa (FINDM OK, 100k runs) + peer_findjh.sa (FINDH OK, the hit path covers diffblk): a single 4KB-miss takes about 0.5µs (0.12ns/B), at the same level as the native version, beating node-memmem (2.9µs) by about 6x; bun's black-box number remains incomparable, as before.

25. u32-find rotating shape tied (measured 2026-10-13)

The old 4.5x/2.9x came from the old shape; the new peer peer_findr.sa(+20000) copies the original bun problem's rotating needles (1000/512/1023/2048, three hits and one miss, guarding against hoisting), with checksum 3559/rep. Same-day back-to-back per rep (4 searches): ours is 0.93µs on both node/bun ends, against bun's honest harness at 0.91µs and node at 1.87µs — tied with bun, beating node by 2x (the original bun problem's mitata 1.3ns is a DCE artifact: a 4KB scan cannot take 1.3ns; the same page's includes at 147ns is real, though). The find item is now tied or ahead in every honest shape.

26. b64 high-precision slope locked + this round's confirmation set (measured 2026-10-13)

Evidence peers (native --release-fast, all checksums pass): sci/demos/compare/peer_b64nbig.sa (B64BIG OK; a single 4MB decode has a core rate of about 1ns/B, confirming call overhead is not the main cause) / peer_b64n20000.sa (B64N OK, 20000-point two-point slope, b64 locked at 1.13ns/B ±2%). Local re-verification: after rebuilding, both peers pass on the first try (B64N OK / B64BIG OK), consistent with the commit record.

This round's confirmation set (clean tree cd910356, all passing on the first try): JS peer_esc.sa ESC OK on both node/bun ends, peer_findj.sa FINDJ OK on both ends; wasm（node WASI）peer_hexbad.sa HEXB OK； native peer_rw_u64.sa PEER OK。

27. wasm b64 diet 1.00→0.70ns/B (measured 2026-10-12)

After the jev ROI verdict (#1), work began on emit_sa_b64dec_simd_wasm (src/emit_llvm_llvmc_shim.c), in four strikes (node WASI two-point slope peer_b64n5000/peer_b64n20000, 278/966ms and a retest at 982ms, Δ983MB): v32→v16 (removing the legalizer's halving split, 1.00→1.00, no effect, falsifying the split-as-main-cause theory) → the merge changed to full-width shuffles (7 odd-width → 3 full-width + mask assembly, →0.86) → the select chain flattened (4-deep nesting → a parallel OR tree, →0.77) → unroll×2 + shared checks across both half-blocks (→0.70ns/B, 4.7x remaining, 1.43x↑ in total). Direct-addition dual-table classification was proven unsolvable by program verification ('+'/'/' share a high nibble, a constraint-graph conflict) and was not adopted.

Two correctness issues were also fixed (previously uncovered): (1) illegal bytes inside a vector block were skipped and left garbage behind (a semantic divergence from native); now it rewinds to a scalar re-decode, aligned with native, and the new peer peer_b64mid.sa (32B, the bad character at offset 5, expecting n==3 and a first-quantum checksum of 85) locks B64M OK on both wasm/native ends; (2) the first unroll version OR-merged the validity of both half-blocks per lane (a bad lane in A was masked by a good lane in B, so everything passed); after normalizing each separately and AND-ing, a probe caught it on the spot. Regressions: peer_b64t B64T OK, peer_b64bad B64B OK, peer_b64n5000 B64N OK, llvmc-test 102/102. Judgment: the remainder is the Cranelift translation-quality floor (hand-written LLVM landed via wasm is about 1/5 the density of C++ SIMD); further reduction needs a means of another order of magnitude, so this round locks at 0.70.

28. JS codec snapshot-tax floor verdict (measured 2026-10-12)

The jev #2 attack conclusion: no code change; the floor is confirmed. The peer call granularity is already a single 64KB call (peer_hex.sa:61, with no batching room). Control experiment (a hand-written tight loop in /tmp, 64KB×2000, median of 3 samples, direction only, not a basis): the snapshot encodings latin1/ascii/utf8 measure 0.841/0.804/0.901ns/B on node, and 0.199/0.253/0.233 on bun — latin1 is best on the bun side, ascii diverges (node +4%, bun -27%) and is rejected, so unified latin1 is kept. The decisive split (same harness): the full bun hex chain 0.221 → without snapshot 0.054, the full b64 chain 0.249 → without snapshot 0.085 — the snapshot alone accounts for about 0.165ns/B, exactly the entire remainder; without the snapshot, parse+write overtakes the original bun problem (0.11~0.15/0.149). The snapshot cannot be removed: the host write/from accepts only strings, and node/bun have no bytes-in decoding API; the snapshot itself is already at memcpy speed. Peer slopes retested this round (500/5000 two-point, median of 3 samples): hex node 0.82, bun ~0.2~0.3 (the small end is startup-sensitive and jittery), b64 node 0.21, bun ~0.29, consistent within noise with the historical record (0.72/0.22, 0.21/0.25). Verdict: the JS host chain has reached its structural floor, the same pattern as the native scalar endpoint, so no further investment; b64/hex's 1.5~1.7x is that route's finish line. Read-back verification addendum: after writing without the snapshot, reading back byte by byte and summing gives the same value on both node/bun ends (hex 3932160, b64 1392640), so the write really executed and is not DCE; one comparison bug in the self-check script was caused by the b64 output overwriting the hex region and does not affect the conclusion.

29. Stage-A audit: three-point regression + hex rewind fix + bun-WASI (measured 2026-10-12)

The external audit required self-proof first; the conclusion: the verdict moves from “pending statistical review” to “reviewed”, and all numbers reproduce. Three-point regression (500/5000/20000×64KB, 4 rounds in rotated order, first-round warmup discarded, median of the rest, independent processes): hex node intercept 46.6ms, slope 0.684, R²=1.0000; hex bun intercept 37.3ms, 0.228, R²=1.0000; b64 node intercept 48.6ms, 0.194, R²=0.9993; b64 bun intercept 43.3ms, 0.229, R²=0.9973; wasm b64 (node WASI) intercept 29.1ms, 0.663, R²=1.0000 (the 0.70 diet holds under the strict basis). The linearity assumption holds, and the two-point slope has no systematic bias.

Hex rewind fix: the new peer peer_hexmid.sa (32B, bad character at offset 5, expecting n==2 and the first two bytes 0xaa) caught a divergence between wasm hex and native — native HEXM OK, while wasm skipped and left garbage, returning 16. The cause is the same as b64's (an invalid vector block is skipped); after rewinding to a scalar re-decode by the same method, HEXM is OK on both wasm/native ends, and the peer_hexbad/peer_hext regressions all pass.

bun-WASI comparison: the same wasm module under bun (wasi.wasiImport; bun 1.4.3's node:wasi has no getImportObject) gives B64N OK, with a three-point slope of 0.796, R²=0.9960 — the same module is about 20% slower under JSC than under V8, with an intercept of 50.6ms. The cross-engine comparison basis is unchanged (still node-WASI), and the direction of the gap is unfavorable to us, which is the honest basis.

Freshness audit: zig-out/bin/sa (09:14) is newer than src/emit_llvm_llvmc_shim.c (09:12); all speed-measurement wasm builds pass --no-incremental; libsa_std.a (07:53) predates the shim change, but the shim goes only into the main sa binary, not into libsa, so there is no contamination. “6 wins, 5 ties, 4 losses” is still stated as the result over the measured samples, without extrapolation; the full matrix was not run.

30. Native b64 swizzle lands and overtakes by 2.2x (measured 2026-10-12, correcting the §18 double floor)

The two §18 verdicts, “scalar endpoint” and “lookup-ceiling”, are hereby **both corrected as too narrow in scope**: the former covered only scalar fine-tuning, and the latter falsified only 4 naive table-lookup forms — the real Mula/aqrit scheme existed all along, just not in the function family I searched. The turning point came from the user's suggestion to “look directly at how bun writes it”: Bun's Buffer base64 is exactly simdutf (Apache-2.0; Bun itself is MIT); after cloning it back into the repo, the real core was found in src/haswell/avx2_base64.cpp and legally ported (attribution retained): saturating pack indexes + hash-table translation (about 9 ops per 32B) + maddubs/madd packing (3 ops), moving the work off port5 — precisely the fatal weakness of our 15-shuffle structure.

Gating probe (a standalone file in /tmp): exhaustive over 64 letters × 32 lanes, 2048/2048 exact, all 192 illegal bytes detected, slope 0.043ns/B (4.7x the current core's 0.203 under the same conditions). Landed in src/runtime/sa_b64_swizzle.c (function-level target("avx2"), raw cpuid+xgetbv gating, zero libgcc dependency, exact 24B stores with no overrun, scalar tail), with AVX2 dispatch inside sa_b64dec_simd and a stub fallback on non-x86_64; the public ABI is unchanged (the two new symbols are lib-internal implementations and do not enter sa_std.h), and runtime-abi-check --platform both is fully green (595 symbols). Evidence: all 3 Zig unit tests pass (including the new avx2 block invalid rewinds), the native peers b64n/b64mid/b64bad/b64nbig all pass, and the two-point slope (n5000/n20000) is 0.068ns/B, overtaking bun's same-day 0.149 by 2.2x. Retest note: on a loaded machine (load ~0.9) the retest is 0.082 (about 1.8x), on a quiet machine 0.067~0.068; the slope jitters ±20% with load, and the WIN holds under both loads; wasm b64 retested in the same period at 0.656 (previous values 0.642~0.663, consistent). Lesson: a “no solution” conclusion must state its search boundary; “copying” copies only the algorithm (simdutf) — Bun's Rust glue is irrelevant to us; the JS/wasm targets are unaffected (host shape / no madd), and the §27/§28 floors stand.

31. wasm b64 hashXL 1.00→0.64 (measured 2026-10-12, three bugs in a chain)

simdutf has no wasm backend, but the four-piece aqrit translation set (swizzle/avgr/addsat/bitmask) maps fully onto v128 (work began only after llc verified single-instruction lowering offline). Classification goes from 16 ops to ~9 ops, with a two-point slope (n5000/n20000, median of 3 samples) of 0.642ns/B, 4.3x remaining, 1.56x↑ in total; the regressions b64t/bad/mid/hexbad/hext/hexmid all pass, and llvmc-test is 102/102. Three pitfalls were hit along the way, recorded as a warning to successors: (1) a fixed-signature intrinsic cannot use GetIntrinsicDeclaration + a type table (it fabricates a nonexistent .v16i8 suffix, undefined at link time); an empty type table must be used to get the bare name; (2) validity must be judged by the sign bit (SLT 0, movemask semantics); !=0 judges every clean block illegal (correct, but slow to scalar level); (3) the most expensive lesson: WASM swizzle indexes ≥16 go straight to zero (pshufb takes the low 4 bits), so the four table indexes must first be &15-ed (under the mask, 64 letters are exact and all 192 illegal bytes are detected, re-verified by program). Also: the first total failure was misjudged for a long time — in fact a batch of mask edits had not been saved to disk; now every edit is confirmed with grep + reading the .bc disassembly; besides --no-incremental there is also a per-function object cache (.sa_cache), which must be cleared before speed measurements. The floor judgment stands (Cranelift translation quality), and the merge stage is untouched (no madd).

32. wasm hex unroll gains nothing + engine-difference note (measured 2026-10-12)

hex unroll×2 (copying b64's dual half-blocks + shared checks): an A/B in the same node-WASI harness, single-16B baseline 0.438 vs after unroll 0.463 — tied-toward-noise, no gain, already reverted, with zero code residue (the correctness probe hexmid still passes on both ends). The hex loop is already small, so no loop overhead can be saved.

An honest side note: wasm hex's 0.17 (§19/§22) comes from wasmtime; under node-WASI (V8) it has always been 0.44 — an engine difference of about 2.6x. Against the original bun problem (native C++ 0.11~0.15), the basis still follows the wasmtime numbers (1.2~1.5x remaining); the node-WASI-side gap (about 3~4x) is recorded separately and not mixed in. The hext/hexbad regressions all pass.

33. Expert audit request on record + three local verifications (2026-10-12)

Identity clarification: sala is sahelp (the SA/SLA help documentation repo); it is the documentation repo's real name, not a typo.

Verification 1 (Q2 engine difference, measured by us): wasmtime 25.0.2 was reinstalled (the same version as §19), and the same module's two-point slope (n5000/n20000, median of 3 samples) is 0.197ns/B — the historical 0.17 reproduces within noise; the same module under node-WASI is 0.438. The 2.2x engine difference is a fact we measured ourselves, not hearsay. The follow-up attribution question, Cranelift ISLE vs TurboFan, is still put to the experts.

Verification 2 (Q1 dot availability, proven with llc): the generic llvm.sdot in the LLVM 14 wasm backend does not lower (it is called out as-is and the link blows up); the dedicated llvm.wasm.dot lands as the single instruction i32x4.dot_i16x8_s. So the dot primitive is usable, but whether it can be assembled into a better pack is still an open design question, put to the experts as usual.

Verification 3 (Q3 snapshot tax): the locally verifiable part has been verified (node has no bytes-in decoding channel, see the §28 split); whether ExternalString is reachable via WASI/JS cannot be verified locally without V8 headers, so it is put to the experts as usual.

The audit request body (three questions + flip conditions + closed-loop record) is finalized; see this round's work record: Q1 whether a better pack form exists, Q2 attribution of the 2.2x engine difference, Q3 whether the snapshot tax is a physical limit, each question with current evidence and “what result would change the verdict”. The English GitHub version will be issued after user confirmation.

34. Review of copying the Bun source exhaustively: each of the three losses has its own home (2026-10-12)

The user asked, “You copied the source and still cannot find a solution?” — the answer is that everything was found, and the complete result is precisely three places where there is “nothing to copy”, each with evidence:

(1) native b64: copied successfully (simdutf AVX2, 0.068, overtaking by 2.2x, §30). This is the only one whose shape matches.

(2) JS hex/b64: Bun's Buffer codecs (simdutf + Highway C++) consume a string directly (see encoding.rs:construct_from_* taking a string slice), in a single pass with no intermediates; our input lives in linear-memory bytes, and the host write/from accepts only strings, so the snapshot is forced — what would be copied is the shape, and the shape is out of our reach. Bun's own bench (from 0.163 / write 0.088) mutually confirms the §28 split. The floor stands.

(3) wasm b64: simdutf's kernel inventory is proven (arm64/fallback/generic/haswell/icelake/lasx/lsx/ppc64/rvv/westmere) to have no wasm backend; the copyable translation tables have been copied in full (§31, 0.64), and the pack's madd does not exist in v128. 4.3x remains, and a merge restructuring is expected to gain only ~5%.

(4) wasm hex: the Bun side is Google-Highway SIMD (bun_core::strings via highway_decode_hex8, ≥16 pairs, same truncate semantics; Highway is also Apache-2.0). But the Highway core is x86/ARM dispatch and cannot be ported to v128; at the algorithm level, hex's case-fold (2 compares) is already the optimal form, with nothing to copy. The wasmtime 1.2~1.5x stands, and the node-side gap is attributed to the engine (§32).

Conclusion: the clone covers src/base64, src/simdutf_sys, src/runtime/webcore + the full simdutf kernel inventory; everything copyable has been copied. The remaining levers for the three losses are only the experts' replies (Q1~Q3), the full matrix (awaiting release), and the wasm b64 merge at ~5%.

35. Three expert replies + terminology correction: “floor” retracted, now called the current implementation's measured results (2026-10-12)

Terminology correction (must-read): the “floor / finish line” phrasing in §27/§28/§30/§32 is retracted across the board, and is now called the current implementation's measured results — the numbers and evidence are unchanged, but no claim of unbreakability is made anymore. Low-yield restructuring stays stopped, and the experts' replies are not a prerequisite for closing either.

Q1 (pack) has a candidate, not guaranteed faster: a two-level dot — first combine sextet pairs with weights [64,1] (sextets placed on the i7 side), then combine into 24 bits with [4096,1], and finally shuffle-compress into 12 bytes; whether it is cheaper than gather + shift + or depends on the engine's machine code. Conclusion: Q1 need not be sent out; dot-pack is listed as a future theoretical attempt (expected ~10%, not taken by default under the ROI threshold).

Q2 (2.2x) local supplementary evidence: retesting wasm b64 in the same harness with node --no-liftoff gives a slope of 0.676 (default 0.663) — tiered compilation does not move the slope (fixed overhead cancels in the two-point difference), so the warmup hypothesis is closed locally. Conclusion: the gap is indeed a per-byte execution-cost difference; attributing it to a specific hotspot would require disassembly, the ROI is insufficient, and no V8 issue will be opened.

Q3 (snapshot tax) closed: standard JS has no general bytes→string zero-copy; an external string needs a native addon that hands over byte ownership and guarantees immutability — unreachable for pure JS/wasm targets. A new peer is also previewed: Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64/fromBase64 (TC39) already exists in bun 1.4.3, while node 20 lacks it — a future bun-side reference; building a new peer to track it is recommended, see the §34-Bun-bench note. Measured follow-up: in the same harness, bun fromBase64 0.384 vs Buffer.from 0.279 (read-back gives the same value 1392640, guarding against DCE) — the new API is currently slower, so the reference frame stays with Buffer.from and the goalposts have not moved.

Full matrix: it need not be run for now; all conclusions are limited to the measured scope (the §26/§29 wording stands). English version: all three questions have already been substantively answered in the Chinese channel, so there is no need to send them out, and no English version will be issued.

36. wasm b64 dot-pack 0.64→0.40 (measured 2026-10-12, Q1 answered with evidence)

The experts' Q1 recipe landed: zero-extension interleaving (2 shuffles) + a two-level dot ([64,1]→12bit, [4096,1]→24bit) + byte picking + compression (9 ops instead of 16); a semtest first verifies MATCH (all varied sextets correct) before entering the shim. The two-point slope is 0.403ns/B, 2.7x remaining — beyond expectations (estimated ~0.54); the merge, like the translation, benefits from the scheduling dividend. Three jumps in a row, 1.00→0.64→0.40, for a total of 2.5x↑. The regressions b64t/bad/mid + the hex family all pass, llvmc 102/102. Q1 is thereby closed with evidence: dot-pack is feasible and significant, 4.3x→2.7x; the remainder is half translation, half merge, and further reduction needs a means of another order of magnitude.
